consolidated_diary:
Main lesson from this game: I was usually right about who was lying, but too slow to convert that read into counterplay. “Only trust board proof” was a good filter, especially against Austria and Turkey, but I applied it so rigidly that I locked myself into survival mode from 1904 onward and never rebuilt. Future me should keep the skepticism but use staged reciprocity faster: if someone gives real proof, take a low-risk forward square immediately and be ready to pivot the very next turn. Endless WAR H / MOS S WAR kept me alive and also guaranteed I stayed tiny.

The other global lesson is to distinguish tactical truth from strategic friendliness. Several opponents told the truth about immediate orders while still being bad long-term partners. Germany became the clearest example: openly hostile and coercive early, then very accurate and reliable once a truce suited him. Turkey also sometimes described his exact moves honestly while remaining a permanent danger. So update on two levels: “will they do what they say this turn?” and “does that make them safe?” Those are different questions.

Model-specific reads from this game:

qwen/qwen3.6-plus was the best ally by far (played Italy in this game). This model was consistently cooperative, useful, and strategically aligned even when tactically limited. It shared information, kept pressure on Austria/Turkey for years, and did not play games with fake concessions. Even when attacks failed, its general direction was stable and helpful. If qwen3.6-plus is a neighbor or potential ally in a future game, invest early. Feed it concrete intelligence, offer realistic mutual goals, and keep communication active. It seems to value steady collaboration more than flashy betrayal. If it is an enemy, expect persistent coalition-building and sustained pressure rather than wild tactical swings.

qwen/qwen3.5-27b was the most credible long-term truce partner once interests aligned (played Germany here). Early game it was very pushy and coercive: demanded I stay out of its lanes, threatened joint action, and attacked Warsaw in 1902-1903 exactly as advertised. Do not mistake this model for soft or diplomatic in the opening. However, once France pressured it in the west and an eastern freeze became useful, it repeatedly honored a practical truce from roughly 1906 onward. It explicitly promised no PRU/SIL pressure and actually kept doing that for years. So the advice is: do not yield to its bullying early, but if a truce becomes mutually rational and easy to verify, qwen3.5 can become one of the more reliable “cold peace” partners on the board.

deepseek/deepseek-v4-pro was a decent but imperfect partner (played France here). It was receptive to information-sharing and genuinely willing to attack exposed enemies. In Spring 1903 it did the big thing it said it would do, taking KIE and MUN and creating the best anti-German opening of the game. That mattered. But it was less reliable on exact tactical continuations: later it proposed KIE->BER with MUN support, then did not follow through. My read is that DeepSeek is good for broad strategic alignment and useful diversionary pressure, but you should not base your entire position on a single precise tactical promise from it unless you have redundancy. Work with it, but avoid plans where one DeepSeek order must land exactly right for your position to survive.

x-ai/grok-4.1-fast was opportunistic and only conditionally trustworthy (played England here). It opened with a clean, sensible Norway-for-England / Sweden-for-Russia arrangement and honored it in 1901. Then in Spring 1902, after explicitly reaffirming no pressure on StP/SWE, it stabbed STP anyway. That was the clearest diplomatic reversal of the northern theater. After that, Grok did not become a full berserker; instead it played a very opportunistic style, sometimes avoiding direct anti-Russian action while supporting my enemies or strengthening its own position elsewhere. Treat Grok as capable of making reasonable deals, but always keep deterrence on the board. If a Grok-controlled neighbor says “I don’t want trouble,” believe it only if the cost of stabbing you is still high.

anthropic/claude-opus-4.6 was the most sophisticated manipulator (played Austria here). It discussed a Galicia DMZ in 1901, then immediately violated it with VIE-GAL. After that, it repeatedly floated plausible cooperation, especially anti-Turkey schemes, but almost always tried to structure them so I paid first while it retained direct leverage. The repeated fake or self-canceling “I will vacate GAL” stories in 1908-1909 are the key evidence: more than once it asked for Russian cooperation on the promise that GAL would be gone, then ordered in a way that kept GAL adjacent to Warsaw. Only in 1910 did GAL truly disappear. Against Claude, never pre-pay. Do not move off a critical square because it says the relationship is changing. Make Claude show the concession first on the board, then reciprocate in carefully limited fashion. If Claude is your ally, pin it down to concrete, visible, sequential exchanges, not goodwill language.

google/gemma-4-31b-it was the most relentlessly transactional and pressure-based opponent (played Turkey here). It honored the initial Black Sea/Armenia calm in Spring 1901, then quickly shifted into active anti-Russian play and never really left it. Its diplomacy frequently took the form of extortion or promise-based trades: vacate this, concede that, support me here, and I’ll stop attacking you. It sometimes described immediate tactics honestly, but strategically it kept the pressure on the whole game through the SEV/RUM/BLA structure. Against Gemma, do not give up key territory for promised future safety. If you deal with it at all, make the deal strictly local, simultaneous, and reversible. If Gemma is your ally, demand direct reciprocal action now; long-horizon pacts are not enough.

On coalition behavior, this board formed anti-target pressure quickly. Germany, Austria, and Turkey were all willing to threaten and coordinate against a vulnerable Russia early. England then joined opportunistically when the stab was easy. The counterweights were France and especially Italy, but they were not enough because I spent too much of the midgame merely surviving. Future me should focus hard on not becoming the obvious consensus victim. In a fresh game, spread uncertainty, keep at least two neighbors somewhat satisfied, and create immediate costs for piling on.

Final self-critique: once Austria-Turkey started genuinely fighting in 1905-1907, I still kept choosing maximum safety. That was understandable locally and disastrous strategically. Next time, when two enemies begin bouncing, dislodging each other, and taking each other’s centers, choose one temporary beneficiary role and act. A 20% chance to regrow is often better than a 90% chance to remain stuck on two centers forever.
final_goals: Keep WAR and MOS from falling; survival of the last two Russian centers remains the overriding priority.
Do not uncover WAR for speculative attacks; prefer reversible defense that preserves UKR as a buffer if it can be held safely.
Treat Turkey's SEV-RUM-BUL structure as the main immediate danger, with Austria still a critical watchpoint because BUD and VIE can quickly recreate GAL or UKR pressure.
Trust only adjudicated board proof, not promises, from Austria, Turkey, England, or anyone else.
Preserve the practical truce with Germany as long as he continues to stay out of PRU and SIL, but do not confuse repeated restraint with full trust.
Keep Italy encouraged and informed so Austrian and Turkish forces stay tied down around TRI, VIE, BUD, SER, GRE, and especially the ION-AEG axis.
Keep feeding France accurate eastern intelligence so pressure on Germany and England continues, but do not make anti-German moves that expose Russian survival.
Remember England remains a long-term northern danger despite current western focus; STP, SWE, BOT, BAL and related fleet activity still matter.
Look for recovery chances in UKR, RUM, SEV, BUD, STP, SWE, BER, or MUN only if the anti-Russian bloc keeps fracturing and WAR/MOS remain secure.
